title: Sentence structure
note: A sentence needs a subject and a predicate and must express a complete thought. A clause has its own subject and verb: an independent clause can stand alone, a dependent clause cannot. Simple sentences have one independent clause, compound sentences two or more, complex sentences one plus a dependent clause.

read.title: The skeleton of a sentence
text: Every English sentence is built on a frame of subject and predicate. The subject names who or what the sentence is about; the predicate says something about it. In "The old ferry crossed the river," the subject is the old ferry and the predicate is crossed the river. Inside the predicate, river is the direct object: it receives the action of crossed.

Clauses are the next level up. A clause is any word group with its own subject and verb. "The ferry crossed the river" can stand alone, so it is an independent clause. "Although the ferry crossed the river" cannot; the word although makes it dependent, and the reader waits for the rest.

Combining clauses gives the main sentence types. One independent clause makes a simple sentence. Two independent clauses, joined by a comma and a word such as and or but, make a compound sentence. An independent clause plus a dependent clause makes a complex sentence. When writers lose track of this frame, they produce fragments, which lack a complete clause, or comma splices, which join two complete clauses with only a comma.
